props.title: Black Lizard

sections.content: Black Lizard stands as one of Japanese cinema's most audacious crime thrillers, directed by Kinji Fukasaku and starring drag queen Akihiro Maruyama (stage name Miwa) as the seductive jewel thief Black Lizard. Based on Yukio Mishima's adaptation of Edogawa Rampo's novel, the film gleefully blends film noir, camp aesthetics, and avant-garde theater. Mishima himself appears in a cameo as a human statue, adding to the film's fascinating intersection of high art and pulp sensibilities. The film's elaborate set designs and costumes create a psychedelic dreamscape that perfectly captures late 1960s Japanese experimental cinema.

sections.content: The influence of Black Lizard can be traced through later Japanese genre-bending films like Pistol Opera (2001) and Memories of Matsuko (2006). Its bold mixing of high and low culture, along with its celebration of gender fluidity, prefigured much of contemporary Japanese extreme cinema. The film shares DNA with earlier experimental noir like Pale Flower (1964) while pointing toward the baroque excess of directors like Sion Sono. SUBHEAD: Crime and Camp in Japanese Cinema

The film exists in fascinating dialogue with other Japanese crime films that play with gender and sexuality, from Funeral Parade of Roses (1969) to Gohatto (1999). Director Kinji Fukasaku would later become known for more straightforward crime films like Battles Without Honor and Humanity (1973), making Black Lizard a unique entry in his filmography. The film's influence can also be seen in contemporary queer Japanese cinema like Close-Knit (2017).
